correctness.rationale: The claim restricts n to squarefree positive integers and uses F(n)=sum_{d|n}d^{-2}=prod_{p|n}(1+p^{-2}); this is not the unrestricted ordinary or unitary divisor range. For primes q>=5, the log weights w_p=log(1+p^{-2}) satisfy w_p<sum_{q>p}w_q: independently recomputed exact rational finite product inequalities for p=5,7,11,13,17,19,23; for p>=29 Nagura supplies q_i<(6/5)^i p, then sum log(1+q^{-2})>25/[11(p^2+1)]>p^{-2}>log(1+p^{-2}). The explicit greedy infinite binary-subsum lemma therefore gives all log values in [0,sum_{p>=5}w_p], and finite products are dense, hence the prime tail interval [1,R] with R=prod_{p>=5}(1+p^{-2})=54/(5*pi^2). Independent omission/inclusion of primes 2,3 multiplies by 1,10/9,5/4,25/18. Strict Archimedean pi bounds prove 1<R<10/9<9/8, so all four scaled intervals are disjoint and exhaust the closure. This is a complete infinite argument depending on the known Nagura theorem; finite squarefree samples in checker.py are not accepted as the infinite proof. The disconnectedness is topological closure, not realized values pointwise.
residual_risks: The proof uses Nagura’s classical prime-between-x-and-6x/5 theorem for all real x>=25.
It proves exactly a closure, not that each continuum point is attained by finite squarefree integer n.
